claims.text: Thomas Baekdal's week of Cloudflare AI tracking for baekdal.com showed 16,000 AI answer retrievals and 10 referrals sent back.
claims.quote: came to 16,000. The referrals those answers sent back came to 10.

value.unit: AI answer retrievals in one week

claims.text: By bot: Claude-SearchBot 4,307 requests and no clicks, ChatGPT-User 3,831 and seven, PerplexityBot 3,446 and none, Applebot 2,414 and none, MistralAI-User 1,815 and none.
claims.quote: Claude-SearchBot 4,307 requests and no clicks; ChatGPT-User 3,831 and seven; PerplexityBot 3,446 and none; Applebot 2,414 and none; MistralAI-User 1,815 and none.

claims.text: Baekdal called the pattern predatory and said he is not looking to be paid by AIs; he wants people to come to his site.
claims.quote: I want instead to have people come to my site.

claims.text: The post carries its own caveat: an inconsistent Cloudflare block rule was found afterwards, so the exact figures may move, though the shape does not depend on them.
claims.quote: so the exact figures may move. And the shape does not depend on them.

claims.text: Cloudflare's network-wide data for July 2025 put Anthropic at 38,000 pages crawled for every visitor referred, OpenAI at about 1,100, Perplexity at about 195, against Google's 5.4.
claims.quote: 38,000 pages crawled for every visitor referred

value.unit: pages crawled per visitor referred, Anthropic

claims.text: TollBit counted one AI bot visit for every 31 human visits by the last quarter of 2025, from one in 200 at the start of the year, and 179 bot visits per human referral for European publishers.
claims.quote: 179 bot visits for every human referral an AI app sent back

value.unit: bot visits per human referral, European publishers

claims.text: The usual reading is a tragedy of the commons, and it is right; the second reading is that sixteen thousand fetches are a cost to the fetcher too, spend that already happens.
claims.quote: Sixteen thousand fetches are a cost to the fetcher too.

claims.text: Cloudflare began blocking AI crawlers by default in July 2025 with pay per crawl over HTTP 402, and on 1 July 2026 moved towards paying publishers when their content appears inside an answer.
claims.quote: when their content actually appears inside an answer.

claims.text: By June 2026 bots were 57.4% of all traffic to HTML content on Cloudflare's network.
claims.quote: bots were 57.4% of all traffic to HTML content on its network

value.unit: percent of HTML traffic from bots

claims.text: A layer of pricing machinery was built in a year: RSL, the IAB Tech Lab's protocols, Microsoft's Publisher Content Marketplace, and Perplexity's Comet Plus, which puts 80% of a $5 subscription into a pool.
claims.quote: In the year between those two announcements a whole layer of pricing machinery was built

claims.text: The largest licensing deal is News Corp's, more than $250 million over five years from OpenAI, paid in cash and credits.
claims.quote: more than $250 million over five years from OpenAI

claims.text: Everything on the list prices the content, the fetch or the citation; none of it prices the form the content arrives in and what that form costs the fetcher.
claims.quote: All of it prices the content.

claims.text: Before a fetched HTML page can be shown to a model the provider must parse it, decide which part is the article, strip the rest and tokenise it, billed by the token whether article or cookie banner.
claims.quote: the model is billed by the token whether the tokens are the article or the cookie banner

claims.text: Anthropic's pricing page gives the rule of thumb that an average 10 kB web page is about 2,500 tokens and a 100 kB documentation page about 25,000.
claims.quote: an average 10 kB web page is about 2,500 tokens, a 100 kB documentation page about 25,000

value.unit: tokens per average 10 kB web page

claims.text: Jeremy Howard's llms.txt proposal of September 2024 said an HTML page wraps its information in navigation, ads and JavaScript, and every wasted token costs time and money.
claims.quote: every wasted token costs time and money.

claims.text: Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents example was one of its own blog posts: 16,180 tokens as HTML and 3,150 as markdown, a saving of 81%, with an x-markdown-tokens header.
claims.quote: 16,180 tokens as HTML, 3,150 as markdown, a saving of 81%

claims.text: Cloudflare noted that the agents already asking for markdown are Claude Code and OpenCode, both coding agents, neither a search bot.
claims.quote: Claude Code and OpenCode, both coding agents, neither a search bot

claims.text: On this site the 183 HTML pages come to 1,290,795 tokens and their markdown twins to 488,625, 62% fewer, an average page falling from 7,054 to 2,670 tokens.
claims.quote: the 183 HTML pages come to 1,290,795 tokens and their markdown twins to 488,625

value.unit: percent fewer tokens as markdown, 183 pages

claims.text: On the fourteen articles alone the saving is 53% in total and 64% at the median, long pieces saving least and short ones most.
claims.quote: On the fourteen articles alone the saving is 53% in total and 64% at the median

claims.text: Cloudflare found that more than half of the crawl traffic from bots it classifies as legitimate goes toward re-fetching pages that have not changed.
claims.quote: goes toward re-fetching pages that have not changed.

value.unit: percent (more than half) of legitimate bot crawl re-fetching unchanged pages

claims.text: In a paper with ETH Zurich, more than 90% of the pages processed by large crawlers such as Common Crawl are unique by content, which defeats the web's cache layer.
claims.quote: more than 90% of the pages processed by large crawlers such as Common Crawl are unique by content

value.unit: percent of crawled pages unique by content

claims.text: Wikimedia said in April 2025 that bots were about 35% of its pageviews and 65% of its most expensive traffic: our content is free, our infrastructure is not.
claims.quote: bots were about 35% of its pageviews and 65% of its most expensive traffic

value.unit: percent of Wikimedia's most expensive traffic from bots

claims.text: Sixteen thousand fetches a week of HTML is about 113 million tokens, markdown about 43 million; the difference is 70 million tokens a week, $70 to $350 at list prices.
claims.quote: The difference is 70 million tokens a week.

value.unit: million tokens a week saved for a site like Baekdal's

claims.text: Perplexity prices a URL fetch at $0.0005 on its agent API, so its own list price for Baekdal's 16,000 fetches is about $8 before the tokens.
claims.quote: its own list price for Baekdal's 16,000 fetches is about $8

value.unit: USD for 16,000 fetches at Perplexity's list price

claims.text: The real saving is lower than the arithmetic: providers run an extractor first, cache and use cheaper models where they can, and retrieval often truncates.
claims.quote: there are three reasons the real figure is lower still

claims.text: The argument survives because the extractor is a guess the site knows the answer to, no mitigation touches the re-fetches, whose signal only the publisher can send, and the saving is per site but the spend is across the web.
claims.quote: the saving is per site but the spend is across the web

claims.text: Easy to read has four steps in order of saving: a markdown twin with llms.txt, a date and a hash, frozen hashed sources, and a typed graph; every step exists today and nobody pays for them.
claims.quote: Every step exists today. What does not exist is anyone paying for them.

claims.text: In June 2025 Google's John Mueller said no AI system uses llms.txt; the search bots in Baekdal's list are not asking for markdown, the coding agents are.
claims.quote: The search bots in Baekdal's list are not, as far as anyone can tell, asking for markdown. The coding agents are.

claims.text: The Evidence Dispatch vault hashes every source and ties every correction to the claim it supersedes, so a claim can be walked to its bytes without a second fetch.
claims.quote: so a claim can be walked to its bytes without a second fetch

claims.text: Wikimedia published structured JSON in April 2025 so developers work with the structure instead of scraping article HTML, and Cloudflare's AI Index is the infrastructure version of the same step.
claims.quote: rather than have AI developers scrape article HTML, it published structured JSON

claims.text: A provider that spends fewer tokens reading a site that serves structure has saved money it was already spending, and should hand part of the saving back as a rebate for the format.
claims.quote: A provider that spends fewer tokens reading a site that serves structure has saved money it was already spending, and should hand part of the saving back to the site.

claims.text: The measurement is the easy part: the provider already has the token count per fetch, per domain, per week, and the saving is a number in its own logs.
claims.quote: The saving is a number in its own logs.

claims.text: The rebate can be paid in money over the x402 rail, where a consultant made a site charge a cent a page and Claude Code paid it in test currency, running the other way.
claims.quote: the rebate proposed here is the same rail running the other way

claims.text: Or in tokens: a small publisher can do a great deal with a few million tokens a week, because they are the budget that builds the site, and a marketplace for credits can follow.
claims.quote: If credits are good enough currency for News Corp, they are good enough for baekdal.com.

claims.text: The terms are machine-readable in robots.txt and response headers, as RSL and content signals were built for, and the accounting is per fetch and per domain; nothing needs a new protocol.
claims.quote: Nothing here needs a new protocol.

claims.text: The per-site number is small: seventy dollars a week is a rounding error for OpenAI and a coffee a day for Baekdal, and it will not save journalism.
claims.quote: Seventy dollars a week is a rounding error for OpenAI and a coffee a day for Baekdal.

claims.text: A single site cannot send the invoice; the broker will be whoever sits between the bots and the sites, today Cloudflare, TollBit and the marketplaces.
claims.quote: Baekdal cannot bill Anthropic for serving markdown, and there is no counter to walk up to.

claims.text: Baekdal does not want money and tokens are not an audience; if a publisher's position is that no exchange short of a human reader counts, this proposal does not answer it.
claims.quote: if a publisher's position is that no exchange short of a human reader counts, this proposal does not answer it

claims.text: This site already runs the publisher's half: every page has a markdown twin listed in an llms.txt, every release is stamped with its commit, and the published vaults hold sources frozen and hashed.
claims.quote: If you are reading this in markdown, the saving has already happened.

claims.text: What would settle the hypothesis lives in the providers' logs: per domain for a week, the tokens spent on HTML, the tokens the twin would have cost, and the fetches a change signal would have skipped.
claims.quote: What would settle the hypothesis is the other half, and it lives in the providers' logs.

claims.text: The token measurements were made on 28 September 2026 with the cl100k_base tokenizer over the 183 pages of the site that have markdown twins.
claims.quote: The token measurements were made on 28 September 2026 with the
